# Seizures and epilepsy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Seizure disorders > Seizures and epilepsy*

[Original Article Link](/library/RR0l5f)

---

## Summary

A <u>seizure</u> is a transient manifestation of abnormal excessive or synchronous electrical <u>brain</u> activity that causes <u>convulsions</u>, <u>loss of consciousness</u>, and/or <u>lapses</u> of consciousness. The underlying cause of <u>seizures</u> is a state of neuronal hyperexcitability, which may be temporary (e.g., due to <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances) or long-lasting (e.g., due to inherited or acquired neural abnormalities). <u>Provoked seizures</u> occur as a result of various <u>seizure triggers</u> and underlying conditions (e.g., <u>stroke</u>, <u>traumatic brain injury</u>, <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>), while <u>unprovoked seizures</u> occur in the absence of an identifiable cause. <u>Seizures</u> can also be classified by onset and degree of <u>CNS</u> involvement (e.g., <u>focal seizures</u>, <u>generalized seizures</u>). <u>Epilepsy</u> is a chronic neurological disorder with diagnostic criteria that are based on <u>seizure</u> type, frequency, <u>risk factors</u>, and underlying conditions (e.g., <u>epilepsy syndromes</u>).




Acute complications of <u>seizures</u> include physical trauma and <u>CNS</u> tissue damage due to <u>hyperthermia</u>, cardiorespiratory deficits, or excitatory toxicity. <u>Status epilepticus</u> is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by continuous <u>seizure</u> activity for more than 5 minutes that requires immediate management and stabilization. Acute <u>seizures</u> and <u>status epilepticus</u> in adults and children are most often initially treated with parenteral <u>benzodiazepines</u>, and then with the addition of other parenteral <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>fosphenytoin</u>) if there is no resolution. <u>Rapidly reversible causes of seizures</u> (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u>) should also be managed concurrently. The underlying cause is investigated based on a combination of clinical evaluation (e.g., <u>seizure classification</u>, identifying <u>seizure triggers</u>), <u>laboratory studies</u>, and <u>neuroimaging</u>. <u>Electroencephalography</u> (<u>EEG</u>) can provide additional evidence to support the diagnosis, although a normal <u>EEG</u> between <u>seizures</u> does not rule out <u>epilepsy</u>. Important <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> for the long-term <u>treatment of epilepsy</u> include <u>lamotrigine</u> (first-line treatment in <u>focal seizures</u>), <u>valproate</u> (first-line treatment in <u>generalized seizures</u>), and <u>ethosuximide</u> (first-line treatment in <u>absence seizures</u>). Appropriate medical treatment allows the majority of patients to remain seizure‑free in the long term and prevents long-term complications such as psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, <u>psychosis</u>), <u>sleep disorders</u>, and <u>sudden unexpected death in epilepsy</u> (<u>SUDEP</u>); however, patients must be monitored for adverse effects of medications (e.g., bone disease). <u>Epilepsy</u> in certain groups (e.g., pregnant individuals, children) also may require specific considerations for management.




For information on individual <u>epilepsy syndromes</u>, see “<u>Generalized epilepsy in childhood</u>.”

---

## Definitions

### <u>Seizures</u> [[1]](/library/Dja1ck)




* Seizure: an excessive and/or hypersynchronous activity of cortical <u>neurons</u> that results in transient neurological symptoms

* Acute symptomatic seizure (<u>provoked seizure</u>): a <u>seizure</u> that occurs at the time or soon after the onset of an acute systemic or <u>CNS</u> condition. Examples include: [[2]](/library/NpX-p_)

* Within 1 week of <u>stroke</u>, <u>traumatic brain injury</u> (<u>TBI</u>), <u>anoxic encephalopathy</u>, or intracranial <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Subdural hematoma</u>

* Acute <u>CNS</u> infection

* Exacerbation of <u>multiple sclerosis</u> or other autoimmune diseases

* Metabolic disturbances

* Drug/<u>alcohol intoxication</u> or withdrawal

* Reflex seizure: a <u>seizure</u> constantly evoked by a particular stimulus (trigger) that lowers <u>seizure</u> threshold (e.g., flashing lights; see “<u>Seizure triggers</u>”)

* Unprovoked seizure: a <u>seizure</u> that occurs in the absence of an identifiable cause or beyond the specified interval after an acute <u>CNS</u> condition [[1]](/library/Dja1ck)

* Descriptors: the following terms are used to describe events, clinical features, and <u>EEG</u> signs related to <u>seizures</u> [[3]](/library/cZca0a0)

* Ictal: occurring during a <u>seizure</u>

* Interictal: occurring between the <u>seizures</u>

* Postictal: occurring signs after a <u>seizure</u>





### Epilepsy [[1]](/library/Dja1ck)




* <u>Epilepsy</u>: a chronic neurologic disorder characterized by a predisposition to <u>seizures</u> as defined by one of the following: [[1]](/library/Dja1ck)[[4]](/library/VqbGxu)

* Two or more unprovoked or <u>reflex seizures</u> separated by more than 24 hours

* One unprovoked or <u>reflex seizure</u> in an individual with a high risk of subsequent <u>seizures</u> (e.g., after <u>traumatic brain injury</u>, <u>stroke</u>, <u>CNS</u> infections)

* Diagnosis of an <u>epilepsy syndrome</u>: a group of <u>epileptic disorders</u> characterized by a set of features typically occurring together.

* Common features include triggers, age of onset, <u>EEG patterns</u>, radiological findings, and associated conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u> and other <u>mood disorders</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, and <u>anxiety disorders</u>)

* For more information about individual <u>epilepsy syndromes</u>, see “<u>Generalized epilepsy in childhood</u>.”

* Reflex epilepsy: <u>Epilepsy</u> in which <u>seizures</u> are consistently provoked by a certain trigger (e.g., lights, music, hormonal changes during <u>menstrual cycle</u>). Subtypes can be determined based on the trigger and include:

* Photosensitive epilepsy

* Musicogenic epilepsy

* Catamenial epilepsy

* Drug-resistant epilepsy: <u>epilepsy</u> in which at least two <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> (administered as sequential monotherapies or as combination therapy) have failed to prevent <u>seizures</u>  [[5]](/library/t-XX_00)[[6]](/library/9-XNz00)

* Resolved epilepsy

* An age‐dependent <u>epilepsy syndrome</u> that has not recurred in individuals who are now past the applicable age.

* No recurring <u>seizures</u> for 10 years in individuals who have not taken <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> for at least the last 5 years.





> [!TIP]
> A single <u>seizure</u> or multiple provoked or triggered <u>seizures</u> (e.g., <u>febrile seizures</u>) without an underlying predisposition to <u>seizures</u> do not suffice for the diagnosis of <u>epilepsy</u>.

---

## Etiology

### Seizure triggers [[9]](/library/MtbMVv)




<u>Seizure triggers</u> are stimuli that can precipitate <u>seizures</u> both in people with and without <u>epilepsy</u>. [[10]](/library/yjad1k)




* Excessive physical exertion

* <u>Alcohol</u> consumption

* <u>Fever</u> (<u>febrile seizures</u>)

* <u>Sleep deprivation</u>

* Flashing lights (e.g., strobe lights, video games)

* Music  [[11]](/library/UAXbQ00)

* Hormonal changes (e.g., at different phases of <u>the menstrual cycle</u>, after <u>menopause</u>)

* Medication-related issues in patients with known <u>epilepsy</u>: e.g., <u>poor adherence</u>, recent changes in drug doses or formulation, new medication interactions





### Causes of <u>acute symptomatic seizures</u> [[2]](/library/NpX-p_)




* <u>TBI</u>

* <u>Stroke</u>

* <u>Anoxic encephalopathy</u>

* Intracranial <u>surgery</u>

* Acute <u>CNS</u> infections (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>, <u>encephalitis</u>)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalance (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>)

* Acute metabolic disturbances (e.g., <u>uremia</u>)

* <u>Alcohol withdrawal</u>

* <u>Recreational drug</u> use

* Prescription drug toxicity

* Exacerbations of autoimmune disorders (e.g., <u>SLE</u>)





### Common causes of <u>epilepsy</u> [[12]](/library/ZPaZWk)




* Genetic

* Genetic mutations affecting ion channels or transmitter <u>receptors</u> (e.g., mutations in KCNQ2 or SCN1A <u>genes</u>)

* <u>Chromosomal abnormalities</u> (e.g., <u>Angelman syndrome</u>, <u>Prader-Willi syndrome</u>, <u>Rett syndrome</u>)

* Genetic metabolic disorders (e.g., <u>PKU</u>, congenital disorders of <u>glycosylation</u>, <u>lysosomal storage diseases</u>, peroxisomal biogenesis disorders)

* <u>Mitochondrial</u> diseases (e.g., <u>MELAS</u>)

* Structural: chronic cerebral lesion or abnormality

* <u>Perinatal</u> injury, e.g., <u>hypoxic</u>-<u>ischemic</u> injury

* <u>Brain tumors</u> and <u>metastases</u> [[13]](/library/5tbiVv)

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u> (<u>TBI</u>)

* Hippocampal <u>sclerosis</u>

* <u>Tuberous sclerosis</u>

* Congenital cerebral or <u>arteriovenous malformations</u>

* <u>Microcephaly</u>, megalocephaly, cortical dysgenesis

* <u>Cranial</u> <u>radiation therapy</u>

* Metabolic

* <u>Inborn errors of metabolism</u> (e.g., <u>organic acidemias</u>, <u>phenylketonuria</u>)

* <u>Porphyrias</u>

* Immune: <u>autoimmune encephalitides</u> (e.g., <u>anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis</u>), <u>Rasmussen encephalitis</u>

* Infectious: : chronic <u>CNS</u> infection (e.g., <u>toxoplasmosis</u>, <u>malaria</u>, <u>neurocysticercosis</u>) or complication of acute <u>CNS</u> infection (e.g., viral or <u>bacterial meningitis</u> or <u>encephalitis</u>)





### Causes of <u>epilepsy</u> according to the age group [[14]](/library/LgYwDo)




| Etiology of <u>epilepsy</u> in different age groups |  |
| --- | --- |
| Age group at manifestation | Causes |
| <u>Neonates</u> and <u>infants</u> (< 6 months) | <br><br>* Genetic<br><br>* Congenital structural maldevelopment (e.g., <u>microcephaly</u>, megalocephaly)<br><br>* <u>Perinatal</u> injury<br><br>* <u>Perinatal</u> or postnatal infections (e.g., <u>CNS</u> infections)<br><br>* Metabolic disorders (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>PKU</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>)<br><br>* In <u>infants</u> aged 1–6 months: <u>West syndrome</u><br><br><br> |
| Older <u>infants</u> (> 6 months) and children (< 10 years) | <br><br>* <u>Febrile seizures</u><br><br>* Genetic (e.g., Rolandic <u>epilepsy</u>)<br><br>* Infections<br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* Congenital <u>brain</u> <u>malformations</u> (e.g., cortical dysgenesis)<br><br>* Metabolic disorders<br><br>* Accidental drug <u>poisoning</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Adolescents</u> (10–18 years) | <br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* <u>Encephalitis</u><br><br>* Genetic disorders<br><br>* Illicit substance use<br><br><br> |
| Adults (18–60 years) | <br><br>* <u>Alcohol withdrawal</u><br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* Illicit substance use<br><br>* <u>Brain tumors</u><br><br>* Infection<br><br>* Metabolic disorders<br><br><br> |
| Older adults (> 60 years) | <br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebrovascular disease</u><br><br>* <u>Brain tumors</u><br><br>* <u>Abscesses</u><br><br>* <u>Neurodegenerative diseases</u><br><br><br> |

## Classification

### Classification of seizures according to the <u>ILAE</u> 2017 classification [[15]](/library/Ctbqfv)




<u>Seizures</u> are classified according to localization of abnormal neuronal activity and then further subcategorized based on symptoms and sometimes level of awareness.




| Basic <u>classification of seizures</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Focal | Generalized | Unknown |
| Location of abnormal neuronal activity | <br>* Originates within the networks of a single hemisphere<br><br> | <br>* Originates from both hemispheres<br><br> | <br>* Determination of focal or generalized onset is not possible<br><br> |
| Awareness | <br><br>* Aware<br><br>* Impaired awareness<br><br><br> | <br>* N/a<br><br> | <br>* N/a<br><br> |
| Symptoms | <br><br>* Motor onset<br><br>* Nonmotor onset<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Motor<br><br>* <u>Tonic-clonic</u><br><br>* Other motor<br><br>* Nonmotor<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Motor<br><br>* <u>Tonic-clonic</u><br><br>* Other motor<br><br>* Nonmotor<br><br><br> |
| Other | <br>* Focal to bilateral <u>tonic-clonic</u>: focal progresses to a <u>tonic-clonic</u> pattern (characteristic of bilateral <u>brain</u> involvement)<br><br> | <br>* N/a<br><br> | <br>* Unclassified [[16]](/library/9tbNfv)<br><br> |
| * Note: An expanded version of the <u>ILAE</u> 2017 classification also considers further subtypes of motor and nonmotor categories. |  |  |  |





### Classification of epilepsy [[12]](/library/ZPaZWk)




* General considerations

* The International League Against <u>Epilepsy</u> (<u>ILAE</u>) recommends a multilevel approach to classifying <u>epilepsy</u>.

* Etiology and comorbidities should be considered at each level of classification.

* Levels of classification

* For level 1, first determine the <u>seizure</u> type (see “<u>Classification of seizures</u>” above).

* For level 2, then determine the <u>epilepsy</u> type, which can be:

* Focal

* The lobe from which <u>seizures</u> originate should be determined.

* <u>Epilepsy</u> with focal-to-bilateral <u>tonic-clonic seizures</u> is classified as focal.

* Generalized: diagnosed in patients with generalized-onset <u>seizures</u> as evidenced by generalized <u>ictal</u> activity (e.g., 3 Hz spike-wave activity in <u>absence seizures</u>) and/or typical <u>interictal</u> discharges on <u>EEG</u>.

* Combined generalized and focal: diagnosed in patients who have both focal-onset and generalized-onset <u>seizures</u> (seen, e.g., in <u>Dravet syndrome</u> and <u>Lennox-Gastaut syndrome</u>)

* Unknown: diagnosed if there is not enough clinical information to classify <u>seizures</u> as focal, generalized, or combined

* For level 3, consider <u>epilepsy syndromes</u> (see “<u>Focal seizures and syndromes</u>” and “<u>Generalized epilepsy in childhood</u>” for discussion of specific syndromes)

---

## Clinical features

### Focal seizures (formerly <u>partial seizures</u>) [[10]](/library/yjad1k)[[15]](/library/Ctbqfv)[[17]](/library/l5Yv4p)




* Originate in one <u>brain</u> hemisphere [[18]](/library/wtbhfv)

* Usually caused by focal structural abnormalities

* Symptoms depend on the anatomical location of the lesion or disturbance within the <u>brain</u>.

* For more information about the etiology and symptoms of <u>seizures</u> originating from the cortex of particular <u>brain</u> lobes, see “<u>Focal seizures and syndromes</u>.”





| Clinical features of <u>focal seizures</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Awareness | <u>Ictal</u> | <u>Postictal</u> |
| Focal | <br><br>* May manifest with intact or impaired awareness<br><br>* <u>Focal seizures with impaired awareness</u> most frequently originate from the <u>temporal lobe</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Prodromal</u> symptoms: aura  [[19]](/library/LRawn4)<br><br>* Neuropsychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>, fear, déjà vu)<br><br>* Usually lasts seconds to minutes<br><br>* Aware <u>seizures</u> and <u>seizures</u> with impaired awareness are possible<br><br>* Motor symptoms<br><br>* Automatisms (e.g., lip smacking, blinking, tapping, exploratory movements with hands)<br><br>* Abrupt loss of tone in a muscle group (<u>atonic seizure</u>)<br><br>* <u>Myoclonus</u>: brief involuntary twitching of muscle groups<br><br>* Clonic, involuntary, repetitive movements of the <u>contralateral</u> limbs or facial muscles.<br><br>* <u>Tonic</u> contraction of the <u>contralateral</u> limbs<br><br>* <u>Jacksonian march</u> (march of <u>convulsions</u>): progressive involvement of different muscle groups<br><br>* Irregular large amplitude movements such as pedaling, jumping, <u>pelvic</u> thrusting (hyperkinetic <u>seizure</u>)<br><br>* Nonmotor symptoms<br><br>* Autonomic (e.g. flushing, sweating)<br><br>* Behavioral arrest<br><br>* Cognitive (e.g., <u>dyslexia</u>, <u>aphasia</u>, <u>anomia</u>, <u>anterograde amnesia</u>)<br><br>* Emotional (e.g., laughing, crying, feeling fear)<br><br>* Sensory <br><br>* Visual (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>, micropsia, macropsia)<br><br>* Somatosensory (e.g., <u>paresthesias</u>)<br><br>* Vestibular (e.g., <u>vertigo</u>)<br><br>* Auditory (i.e., <u>hearing</u> simple sounds like ringing)<br><br>* Olfactory (e.g., unusual or intense smells)<br><br>* <u>Gustatory hallucinations</u><br><br>* See “<u>Focal seizures and syndromes</u>” for features according to cortical origin.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Residual transient neurologic deficits depending on the affected cerebral region<br><br>* Todd paralysis: <u>postictal weakness</u> or <u>paralysis</u> of the involved limb or facial muscles (can last for minutes or up to 36 hours)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Focal to bilateral <u>tonic-clonic</u><br> | <br>* Progresses to <u>loss of consciousness</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Prodromal</u> <u>aura</u> may be present.<br><br>* Starts as unilateral, localized focal symptoms that then progress into a bilateral generalized phase: Initial focal symptoms may go unnoticed if the condition progresses rapidly, leading to a potential misdiagnosis of <u>generalized-onset seizures</u> and inappropriate therapy.<br><br>* Bilateral generalized phase<br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u><br><br>* Motor symptoms: See “<u>Tonic-clonic seizure</u>” in the table below.<br><br>* <u>Bladder</u> or <u>bowel incontinence</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Confusion<br><br>* Drowsiness<br><br>* <u>Agitation</u><br><br>* Fatigue<br><br>* May not recall the focal onset<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> If focal to bilateral <u>tonic-clonic</u> type progresses rapidly to the bilateral generalized phase, initial focal symptoms may go unnoticed, leading to a potential misdiagnosis of <u>generalized-onset seizures</u> and inappropriate therapy.




### Generalized-onset seizures [[10]](/library/yjad1k)[[20]](/library/U30b3f)[[21]](/library/YianJ4)




* Involve one/both hemispheres

* Start with <u>loss of consciousness</u>.

* Patients do not recall the <u>seizure</u>.





| Clinical features of <u>generalized seizures</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | <u>Ictal</u> | <u>Postictal</u> |
| Generalized motor <u>seizure</u> |  |  |
| Tonic-clonic seizure (<u>grand mal</u>) | <br><br>* <u>Prodromal</u> symptoms may occur up to hours before <u>seizure</u> onset (e.g., <u>sleep</u> disturbances, <u>lightheadedness</u>, mood changes, <u>anxiety</u>/irritability, impaired concentration)<br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u> (sudden and without warning)<br><br>* Motor symptoms<br>1. * <u>Tonic</u> phase<br><br>* Generalized muscle contractions: rotated eyes, <u>apnea</u>, <u>lateral</u> <u>tongue</u> biting, pooled oral secretions, <u>cyanosis</u>, and characteristic loud moan (<u>ictal</u> cry)<br><br>* Increased <u>sympathetic</u> tone: dilated, unresponsive <u>pupils</u>, ↑ <u>heart rate</u>, ↑ blood pressure<br>2. * Clonic phase: rhythmic muscle twitching<br><br>* <u>Bladder</u> or <u>bowel incontinence</u><br><br>* <u>Tongue</u>-bite <u>lacerations</u><br><br>* Usually lasts 1–3 minutes<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Unresponsiveness<br><br>* Confusion<br><br>* <u>Amnesia</u> of the event<br><br>* <u>Aphasia</u><br><br>* Fatigue<br><br>* Muscular flaccidity and muscle <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* <u>Hypersalivation</u> with or without <u>airway obstruction</u><br><br><br> |
| Clonic seizure | <br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u><br><br>* Bilateral rhythmic jerking (of the entire body or only a part)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Amnesia</u> of the event<br><br> |
| Tonic seizure | <br><br>* Often occurs when the patient is drowsy, asleep, or after waking<br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u><br><br>* Muscle stiffening (extension or <u>flexion</u> of the head, trunk, and/or extremities)<br>* Contraction can be bilateral or unilateral<br><br>* Can be accompanied by autonomic symptoms (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, flushing)<br><br>* Can be followed by <u>atypical absence seizure</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Amnesia</u> of the event<br><br>* Drowsiness or confusion may occur<br><br><br> |
| <br>Myoclonic seizure<br> | <br><br>* <u>Positive myoclonus</u>: sudden jerk-like muscle twitching<br><br>* <u>Negative myoclonus</u>: a brief loss of muscle activity during <u>tonic</u> contraction of a muscle<br><br>* <u>Myoclonus</u> can affect the entire body or only a part.<br><br>* <u>Myoclonic seizures</u> are nonrhythmic (i.e., jerks occur at different intervals) and irregular (i.e., jerks are asymmetric and may change laterality)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Amnesia</u> of the event<br><br> |
| <br>Myoclonic-atonic seizure<br> | <br>* <u>Myoclonus</u> followed by a brief loss of tone<br><br> |  |
| <br>Myoclonic-tonic seizure<br> | <br>* <u>Myoclonus</u> followed by a brief increase in tone<br><br> |  |
| <br>Atonic seizure (also known as “<u>drop seizure</u>” or “<u>drop attack</u>”)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden loss of muscle tone: sudden head drop or collapse (lasts < 15 seconds)<br><br>* Frequently mistaken for <u>syncope</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Generalized nonmotor <u>seizure</u> (<u>absence seizure</u>)<br> |  |  |
| Typical | <br><br>* Interrupted motion or activity, blank stare, unresponsiveness<br><br>* Can occur several hundred times a day and usually lasts < 10 seconds<br><br>* Subtle <u>automatisms</u> (often go unnoticed): lip-smacking, <u>eye</u> fluttering, or head nodding are common.<br><br>* Sudden onset and stop<br><br>* Triggers: <u>hyperventilation</u>, flashing lights<br><br><br> | <br><br>* None<br><br>* Consciousness returns rapidly, without any impairment<br><br>* <u>Amnesia</u> is common<br><br><br> |
| Atypical | <br><br>* Interrupted motion or activity, blank stare<br><br>* Patients may be responsive<br><br>* <u>Automatisms</u>: lip-smacking, <u>eye</u> fluttering, chewing<br><br>* Small hand movements (e.g., rubbing of the fingers)<br><br>* Longer than typical form (10–30 seconds)<br><br>* Gradual onset and stop<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> It is important to distinguish between focal/bilateral <u>tonic-clonic seizures</u> and <u>generalized tonic-clonic seizures</u>, as they manifest similarly but are managed differently.

---

## Diagnosis

The following addresses evaluation following the resolution of an acute <u>seizure</u>. See “<u>Management of acute seizures and status epilepticus</u>” for actively seizing patients.




### Approach




* First <u>seizure</u>

* Confirmation of <u>seizure</u>: Determine if the patient had a true <u>seizure</u> (see also “<u>Differential diagnosis of a seizure</u>”).

* If possible, identify the underlying cause at the initial presentation.

* Clinically evaluate the type of <u>seizure</u> (e.g., <u>focal seizure</u> vs. generalized <u>tonic-clonic seizure</u>) and identify potential <u>seizure triggers</u>.

* Obtain laboratory tests to identify metabolic abnormalities.

* Consider <u>neuroimaging</u> to evaluate for structural causes.

* Obtain an <u>EEG</u>.  [[22]](/library/N11-Sf0)

* Previously diagnosed <u>epilepsy</u>

* Assess for common causes of <u>breakthrough seizures</u> and increased <u>seizure</u> frequency, e.g.: [[23]](/library/vRcAKX0)

* <u>Poor adherence</u> and other medication-related issues

* Intercurrent infection or systemic illness

* <u>Alcohol</u> consumption and/or <u>recreational drug</u> use

* Check <u>antiepileptic drug</u> levels.

* Consider further investigations based on clinical suspicion, e.g., <u>septic workup</u>, selective <u>neuroimaging</u>.  [[23]](/library/vRcAKX0)

* Consider <u>EEG</u> for patients with treatment-refractory <u>seizures</u>, those who have had a change in <u>seizure</u> type, or if there is insufficient information for <u>seizure classification</u>.





> [!TIP]
> In patients with an <u>epilepsy</u> diagnosis who present with an acute <u>seizure</u>, evaluate for medication-related issues, e.g., adherence, changes in drug doses or formulations, medication interactions.




> [!WARNING]
> Obtain <u>neuroimaging</u> in patients with an <u>epilepsy</u> diagnosis if there is a change in <u>seizure</u> pattern or other concerning features are present (e.g., recent <u>head injury</u>, new neurological deficit, persistent <u>headache</u>). [[23]](/library/vRcAKX0)




### Confirmation of <u>seizure</u>




* History

* <u>History of present illness</u>: description of the event by the patient (aware <u>seizure</u>) and/or witnesses (<u>seizure</u> with impaired awareness)

* Potential triggers (e.g., <u>sleep deprivation</u>, excessive <u>alcohol</u> intake)

* <u>Prodromal</u> symptoms (e.g., <u>aura</u>)

* <u>Ictal</u> symptoms

* <u>Postictal</u> symptoms

* <u>Past medical history</u>

* History of <u>epilepsy</u> (including current <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> and adherence)

* History of other potential underlying conditions (e.g., <u>head trauma</u>, <u>stroke</u>, <u>tumor</u>, <u>CNS</u> infection)

* <u>Physical examination</u>: attention should be paid to visual inspection (e.g., for <u>bruises</u> from falls, <u>tongue</u> bites, <u>phakomatosis</u>-specific <u>skin</u> manifestations) and evaluation for cardiovascular disorders

* <u>EEG</u>

* Performed in individuals who present with first <u>seizure</u>, with insufficient information for <u>seizure classification</u>, and/or treatment-refractory <u>seizures</u>

* Characteristic <u>EEG</u> findings help to establish the diagnosis of <u>epilepsy</u>; the absence of such findings cannot, however, rule out <u>epilepsy</u>.

* During the <u>seizure</u> (<u>ictal</u>)

* Epileptiform discharges (e.g., spikes, <u>sharp waves</u>, spike waves) are usually detected.

* Certain types of conditions characterized by <u>seizures</u> have characteristic discharge patterns (e.g., <u>hypsarrhythmia</u> in <u>West syndrome</u>, 3 Hz <u>spike-and-wave</u> in typical <u>absence seizures</u>, burst suppression in <u>anoxic encephalopathy</u> or <u>barbiturate</u> administration)

* If no epileptiform discharges are detected during a <u>seizure</u>, alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>psychogenic nonepileptic seizures</u>) should be considered.

* After a <u>seizure</u> or between <u>seizures</u> (<u>postictal</u> or <u>interictal</u>)

* Often normal findings (even after provocation via <u>sleep deprivation</u>, <u>hyperventilation</u>, or visual stimuli)

* May show epileptiform activity (bursts of abnormal discharges featuring spikes and/or <u>sharp waves</u>, <u>hypsarrhythmia</u> in <u>West syndrome</u>)

* Video-<u>EEG</u> <u>telemetry</u> in hospitalized patients

* Continuous <u>EEG</u> in ambulatory patients





> [!TIP]
> <u>Nonconvulsive status epilepticus</u> is diagnosed based on the clinical presentation (e.g., changes in behavior and/or mental status from baseline) and the demonstration of <u>seizure</u> activity on <u>EEG</u>.




![Anterior temporal spikes and sharp waves](media/zfvbx8gxp4d8uk3f90hbhr5a.jpg)

Anterior temporal spikes and sharp waves




### Evaluation for underlying conditions




* <u>ECG</u>: Rule out cardiogenic causes (e.g., <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u> resulting in cerebral <u>hypoxia</u>) in all patients with <u>loss of consciousness</u> during a <u>seizure</u>.

* <u>MRI</u>: Modality of choice for investigating potential underlying structural abnormalities. [[24]](/library/vAXAl00)

* All patients with first-time <u>focal seizures</u>

* Exception: children with history and examination suggestive of benign <u>seizure</u> or characteristic <u>epilepsy syndrome</u>

* CT: : May be used if <u>MRI</u> is not available, but is less sensitive for identifying soft-tissue lesions [[24]](/library/vAXAl00)

* <u>Angiography</u>: if vascular cause (e.g., cerebral <u>arteriovenous malformation</u>) is suspected

* Laboratory screening: to identify metabolic disorders and infectious diseases, if suspected

* Blood

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Glucose</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u>

* <u>Prolactin</u>

* <u>Toxicology screening</u>

* <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Rapid plasma reagin</u>

* <u>Creatine kinase</u>

* Renal and <u>liver function</u> tests

* <u>Antiepileptic drug</u> levels (e.g., <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>phenobarbital</u>)  [[25]](/library/a11Q2f0)

* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* Bacterial cultures

* <u>Cerebrospinal fluid analysis</u>

* Endocrine studies

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>Adrenal</u> function tests

* <u>Pituitary</u> function tests





![Arteriovenous malformation](media/yqzod9i1bmvcfp7lm60yp1n3.jpg)

Arteriovenous malformation

![Arteriovenous angioma (arteriovenous malformation)](media/hkp2xd95qt132oe5gjglcgwd.jpg)

Arteriovenous angioma (arteriovenous malformation)

![Arteriovenous malformation (angioma)](media/a9aaumdo1wuiewf6y63zap48.jpg)

Arteriovenous malformation (angioma)




> [!TIP]
> In adults, an isolated unprovoked focal or focal to bilateral <u>tonic-clonic seizure</u> typically indicates a structural or metabolic origin and should receive further evaluation.

## Acute management

Acute management steps are determined by the time from <u>seizure</u> onset and include patient stabilization, identification and treatment of reversible acute <u>causes of seizures</u>, and pharmacotherapy to terminate the <u>seizure</u>. Treatment recommendations are consistent with the 2016 American <u>Epilepsy</u> Society (<u>AES</u>) guidelines on the treatment of <u>convulsive</u> <u>status epilepticus</u> in adults and children. [[31]](/library/dQboEt)




### Approach [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[32]](/library/5iciHX0)[[33]](/library/y_XdI00)




* Start <u>initial stabilization steps for acute seizures</u> as needed.

* Identify and treat <u>rapidly reversible causes of seizures</u>.

* Implement phased-based <u>acute seizure management</u>.

* If < 5 minutes from <u>seizure</u> onset: monitor and prepare for <u>benzodiazepine</u> administration.

* If the <u>seizure</u> lasts ≥ 5 minutes (i.e., <u>status epilepticus</u>): ;  [[34]](/library/DRc16X0)

* Urgently administer a parenteral <u>benzodiazepine</u>.

* If no response;  to <u>benzodiazepines</u>: Start a parenteral <u>antiepileptic drug</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Status epilepticus</u> is a life‑threatening condition. If not interrupted, it can lead to <u>cerebral edema</u>, <u>hyperthermia</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>, and cardiovascular failure. If the time from <u>seizure</u> onset is unknown, begin management for <u>status epilepticus</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Acute <u>seizures</u> are often <u>self-limited</u> and may not require immediate pharmacological intervention.

---

## Initial stabilization for acute seizures

* Call for help and remove or control hazards (e.g., remove sharp objects in the patient's vicinity).

* Perform an <u>ABCDE assessment</u>; if needed, perform <u>cardiopulmonary resuscitation</u>.

* Initiate <u>basic airway maneuvers</u>, start <u>oxygen therapy</u>, and place the patient in the <u>recovery position</u>.

* Check <u>POC glucose</u> and <u>vital signs</u>.

* Initiate <u>continuous ECG monitoring</u> if available and start <u>pulse oximetry</u>.

* <u>Obtain IV access</u> and blood samples for investigations.

* Routine: <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u> (including <u>calcium</u> and <u>magnesium</u>), <u>venous blood gases</u>

* Consider also: toxicology screen, <u>blood cultures</u>, <u>pregnancy test</u>, <u>antiepileptic drug</u> levels

* Perform a <u>neurological assessment</u> and collect relevant history.





> [!TIP]
> A severe but <u>self-limited</u> <u>metabolic acidosis</u> due to marked and transient <u>hyperlactatemia</u> commonly occurs immediately after a <u>seizure</u> and usually does not require specific intervention. [[35]](/library/dpcooW0)[[36]](/library/VpcGoW0)




> [!TIP]
> When indicated in an actively seizing patient, a <u>nasopharyngeal airway</u> is preferred over an <u>oropharyngeal airway</u> to avoid damaging intraoral structures in the setting of muscle spasms.

---

## Phase-based acute seizure management

The following addresses <u>acute seizure management</u> in adults and children. For other patient groups see “<u>Neonatal seizures</u>”, “<u>Eclampsia</u>”, or “<u>Febrile seizures</u>.” If initial contact is ≥ 5 minutes from <u>seizure</u> onset or the time from <u>seizure</u> onset is unknown, implement interventions for early <u>seizure</u> and early <u>status epilepticus</u> simultaneously. [[31]](/library/dQboEt)




### Overview




| <br>Overview of pharmacotherapy for acute <u>seizures</u> [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[34]](/library/DRc16X0)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Pharmacotherapy |  |
| <br><u>Seizure</u> phase (time from <u>seizure</u> onset) | Preferred agents | Alternatives |
| <br>Early <u>seizure</u> (0–5 minutes) | <br>* Often <u>self-limited</u>; pharmacotherapy is usually not indicated.<br><br> |  |
| <br>Early <u>status epilepticus</u> (5–20 minutes): first-line therapy Administer push dose.<br>Repeat every 5–10 minutes if no response. | <br><br>* IV <u>benzodiazepine</u> (<u>lorazepam</u> OR <u>diazepam</u>)<br><br>* IM <u>midazolam</u> if <u>IV access</u> is NOT available<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Intranasal <u>midazolam</u><br><br>* Buccal <u>midazolam</u><br><br>* Rectal <u>diazepam</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Persistent <u>status epilepticus</u> (20–40 minutes): second-line therapy Administer <u>loading dose</u>.<br> | <br><br>* IV <u>fosphenytoin</u><br><br>* IV <u>valproic acid</u><br><br>* IV <u>levetiracetam</u><br><br><br> | <br>* IV <u>phenobarbital</u><br><br> |
| <br>Refractory <u>status epilepticus</u> (40–60 minutes) Expert guidance is required.<br> | <br>* Options include repeat second-line therapy or induction of <u>coma</u> (e.g., with IV <u>propofol</u>, <u>thiopental</u>, <u>midazolam</u>, or <u>pentobarbital</u>).<br><br> |  |





> [!WARNING]
> Concurrently manage <u>rapidly reversible causes of seizures</u> (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>) without delay.




![Treatment of status epilepticus](media/krr3yg2klhigl6cd9klszxgw.jpg)

Treatment of status epilepticus




### Early <u>seizure</u> (0–5 minutes)




* Perform <u>initial stabilization for acute seizures</u>.

* Monitor <u>vital signs</u>, <u>oxygen saturation</u>, and <u>ECG</u>.

* Identify and treat <u>rapidly reversible causes of seizures</u>.

* Preemptively prepare for <u>benzodiazepine</u> administration





### Early <u>status epilepticus</u> (5–20 minutes)




Initiate first-line pharmacotherapy with a <u>benzodiazepine</u> (IV route is preferred).




* If <u>IV access</u> is available, administer:

* IV <u>lorazepam</u> DOSAGE [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[38]](/library/a8cQOV0)

* OR IV <u>diazepam</u> DOSAGE [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[34]](/library/DRc16X0)

* If <u>IV access</u> is unavailable, administer one of the following:

* Preferred: IM <u>midazolam</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* Alternatives

* Intranasal <u>midazolam</u> DOSAGE [[34]](/library/DRc16X0)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* OR buccal <u>midazolam</u> DOSAGE [[34]](/library/DRc16X0)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* OR rectal <u>diazepam</u> DOSAGE

* If there is no response to the initial dose, repeat IV <u>benzodiazepine</u> after 5 minutes (after 10 minutes for other routes).

* Monitor for <u>benzodiazepine</u>-induced <u>hypotension</u> and respiratory suppression.

* Consider <u>ICU</u> consult if there is no response to the first dose of <u>benzodiazepine</u>.





### Persistent <u>status epilepticus</u> (20–40 minutes)




If first-line pharmacotherapy is unsuccessful, initiate second-line pharmacotherapy.




* Preferred: <u>loading dose</u> of any ONE of the following 

* IV <u>fosphenytoin</u> DOSAGE  [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[34]](/library/DRc16X0)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* IV <u>valproic acid</u> DOSAGE  [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[34]](/library/DRc16X0)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* IV <u>levetiracetam</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* Alternative: IV <u>phenobarbital</u> DOSAGE [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[37]](/library/yicd8X0)

* If second-line pharmacotherapy successfully stops the <u>seizure</u>, consult <u>neurology</u> regarding the need for <u>maintenance therapy</u>.

* Monitor for medication adverse effects, including: 

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>

* Respiratory <u>depression</u>

* <u>Postictal</u> <u>agitation</u> and/or <u>psychosis</u>

* Prepare for possible <u>intubation</u> and <u>ICU</u> transfer if there is no response to second-line pharmacotherapy.





### Refractory <u>status epilepticus</u> (40–60 minutes)




If first and second-line pharmacotherapy are unsuccessful:




* Consult a specialist: e.g., <u>neurology</u>, anesthesia, and/or critical care.

* Consider:

* Repeat dosing of second-line pharmacotherapy

* Induction of <u>general anesthesia</u> (<u>coma</u>), e.g., with IV <u>propofol</u>, <u>thiopental</u>, <u>midazolam</u>, or <u>pentobarbital</u>.

* Consider <u>intubation</u> and <u>ICU</u> admission.

* Start continuous <u>EEG</u> monitoring.





> [!TIP]
> A recurrent <u>seizure</u> following full neurological recovery from a preceding <u>seizure</u> should be managed as a discrete episode: repeat first-line pharmacotherapy with <u>benzodiazepines</u> while carefully monitoring for respiratory <u>depression</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Focal motor <u>status epilepticus</u> is often drug-resistant but rarely life-threatening. Phase-based management is similar to that of generalized motor <u>seizures</u> but <u>general anesthesia</u> is NOT typically required. [[34]](/library/DRc16X0)

---

## Long-term management

### Long-term management following an isolated seizure [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[32]](/library/5iciHX0)[[33]](/library/y_XdI00)




* Consult <u>neurology</u>.

* Remove cause or provoking factors (e.g., cessation of <u>recreational drug</u> use, treatment of underlying disorders).

* Assess for risk of recurrence; patients with a <u>CNS</u> insult or lesion , abnormality on <u>brain</u> imaging or <u>EEG</u>, or nocturnal <u>seizure</u> are at higher risk of recurrence.

* Low risk of recurrence: <u>shared decision-making</u> with the patient; <u>expectant management</u> is usually appropriate.  [[32]](/library/5iciHX0)[[33]](/library/y_XdI00)

* High risk of recurrence: <u>Treat as epilepsy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Long-term medical therapy following a first <u>unprovoked seizure</u> is not required unless the patient meets the criteria for <u>epilepsy</u> or is at high risk of recurrence.




> [!TIP]
> After the confirmation of <u>PNES</u> diagnosis with video-<u>EEG</u>, <u>anticonvulsants</u> should be withdrawn under medical supervision.




> [!TIP]
> Patients with <u>PNES</u> may benefit from <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>. [[53]](/library/0G1eBR0)




### Long-term management of epilepsy [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[32]](/library/5iciHX0)[[33]](/library/y_XdI00)




* Start, continue, or optimize long-term <u>antiepileptic drugs</u>.

* Monotherapy is preferred unless the <u>seizures</u> are not adequately controlled.

* <u>Drug-resistant epilepsy</u> may be managed with nonpharmacological methods (e.g., <u>surgery</u>, neurostimulation, ketogenic diet).





#### Pharmacotherapy (<u>antiepileptic drugs</u> or <u>AEDs</u>) [[54]](/library/eFbxSv)




* <u>AEDs</u> reduce the risk of future <u>seizures</u> by raising the <u>seizure</u> threshold, which is pathologically lowered in individuals with <u>epilepsy</u>.

* Criteria for the choice of <u>antiepileptic drugs</u>:

* <u>Seizure</u> type

* Patient age

* Comorbidities





| Pharmacotherapy for <u>epilepsy</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Seizure</u> type |  | First line | Second line |
| <br>Focal<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Lamotrigine</u><br><br>* <u>Levetiracetam</u><br><br>* <u>Phenytoin</u><br><br>* <u>Carbamazepine</u><br><br>* <u>Oxcarbazepine</u><br><br>* <u>Phenobarbital</u> (children)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Gabapentin</u><br><br>* <u>Valproate</u><br><br>* <u>Pregabalin</u><br><br>* <u>Topiramate</u><br><br><br> |
| Generalized | <u>Tonic-clonic</u> | <br><br>* <u>Lamotrigine</u><br><br>* <u>Valproate</u><br><br>* <u>Phenobarbital</u> (children)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Carbamazepine</u><br><br>* Zonisamide<br><br><br> |
| Typical absence | <br><br>* <u>Ethosuximide</u><br><br>* <u>Valproate</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lamotrigine</u><br><br>* <u>Clonazepam</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Atypical absence | <br><br>* <u>Valproate</u><br><br>* <u>Lamotrigine</u><br><br>* <u>Topiramate</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Clonazepam</u><br><br>* Felbamate<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Myoclonic</u> |  |  |  |
| Atonic |  |  |  |





##### Treatment regimen




* Monotherapy should be maintained if possible. 

* If initial monotherapy is ineffective, increase the dosage of the single agent or switch to an alternative agent before initiating combination therapy.

* Approx. ⅔ of <u>epilepsy</u> patients become <u>seizure</u>-free with monotherapy. [[55]](/library/17X2kz)

* Combination therapy should only be given if monotherapy fails.

* In this case, drugs from different classes and/or with different pharmacologic modes of action should be tried.

* Combining two or three of the standard <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> is usually safe.

* Failure of combination therapy : Consider nonpharmacological therapy. [[56]](/library/W7XPkz)





##### Termination of treatment




* Evaluated on a case‑by‑case basis

* May be considered if the patient meets all of the following:

* < 2 <u>seizures</u>/year

* An inconspicuous provocation <u>EEG</u>

* Normal psychological findings

* No hereditary predisposition

* Generally possible after 2–5 seizure‑free years with normal <u>EEG</u> results

* Medications should be tapered with caution.





##### Adverse effects of <u>AEDs</u> [[57]](/library/ky1m2j0)[[58]](/library/Ay1R3j0)




See “<u>Overview of AEDs</u>” for agent-specific adverse effects.




* Neurocognitive changes (e.g., sedation, <u>headache</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, <u>tremor</u>, <u>memory</u> impairment)

* <u>Skin</u> disorders (e.g., <u>rash</u>, <u>SJS</u>, <u>DRESS</u>)

* Psychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>psychosis</u>)

* Laboratory abnormalities (e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>neutropenia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>)

* Gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>constipation</u>)

* Weight gain or loss





> [!WARNING]
> In patients with <u>liver</u> disease, hepatically metabolized <u>anticonvulsants</u> (e.g., <u>valproic acid</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>, felbamate, <u>lamotrigine</u>) should be avoided or dose adjusted. [[57]](/library/ky1m2j0)[[59]](/library/VH1G6R0)




#### Nonpharmacological therapy




* Indications: <u>pharmacoresistant epilepsy</u>

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Resection (surgical removal of pathological lesions)

* Patients with <u>temporal lobe epilepsy</u> (e.g., due to hippocampal <u>sclerosis</u>): resection of the anteromedial <u>temporal lobe</u> or of the <u>amygdala</u> and the <u>hippocampus</u>

* Patients with severe intractable <u>seizures</u> due to structural cerebral abnormalities confined to one hemisphere: resection of an entire hemisphere (hemispherectomy)

* Disconnection (surgical section of neuronal circuits)

* Callosotomy: section of the corpus callosum  [[60]](/library/o6X0N_)

* Initially: partial disconnection only (usually the <u>anterior</u> ⅔)

* If <u>seizures</u> persist: complete disconnection

* Hemispherotomy: disconnection of the cortex of one hemisphere from the <u>ipsilateral</u> subcortical structures and cortex of the other hemisphere without removal of the affected hemisphere [[61]](/library/L6Xwl_)

* Stimulation techniques: <u>vagus nerve</u> stimulation, <u>deep brain stimulation</u>

* Dietary measures: ketogenic diet  [[62]](/library/xrXEjz)





> [!TIP]
> Successful <u>epilepsy</u> therapy depends on determining whether the patient has focal or <u>generalized seizures</u> and prescribing medication accordingly.

---

## Complications

### Acute




* <u>Hyperthermia</u>, cardiorespiratory deficits, and excitatory toxicity, which can cause irreversible tissue damage, especially to the <u>CNS</u> (e.g., <u>cortical laminar necrosis</u>) and, in turn, increase the risk of further <u>seizures</u>

* Postictal lactic acidosis: <u>postictal</u> transient <u>anion gap metabolic acidosis</u> with increased <u>lactic acid</u> and reduced serum <u>bicarbonate</u>  (usually resolves spontaneously within 60–90 minutes after <u>seizure</u> activity stops)

* Physical trauma, such as:

* <u>Tongue</u> biting

* <u>Posterior</u> <u>dislocation</u> of the <u>glenohumeral joint</u> due to falling

* <u>Polytrauma</u> from a car accident

* <u>Status epilepticus</u>





![Cortical laminar necrosis](media/yoeapo9jpcla3z5wntqllnje.jpg)

Cortical laminar necrosis




### Long term




* Psychiatric [[63]](/library/u_XpJ00)

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* <u>Depression</u> and risk of <u>suicide</u>

* Cognitive impairment

* <u>Psychosis</u> (interictal psychosis, postictal psychosis, or secondary to <u>antiepileptic drugs</u>)

* Psychosocial <u>distress</u> (e.g., at the workplace)

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbances and <u>insomnia</u>  [[64]](/library/Nbc-Fa0)

* Bone disease (<u>osteomalacia</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>) associated with <u>antiepileptic drugs</u>





### Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (<u>SUDEP</u>) [[65]](/library/n6X7l_)




* The sudden <u>death</u> of a person with diagnosed <u>epilepsy</u> that cannot be attributed to trauma or <u>drowning</u> and occurs with or without evidence of preceding <u>seizure</u> in the absence of any underlying medical conditions that could explain the event

* Usually occurs while the patient is asleep

* Is more common in patients with intractable <u>epilepsy</u>, frequent <u>seizures</u> (especially <u>tonic-clonic seizures</u>), and early age of onset





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Status epilepticus

### Definition [[31]](/library/dQboEt)[[71]](/library/YpXnL_)




* <u>Status epilepticus</u> is a <u>seizure</u> that lasts ≥ 5 minutes or a series of <u>seizures</u> in rapid succession without full neurological recovery in the <u>interictal</u> period, which increases the risk of long-term consequences such as neuronal injury and functional deficits.

* The time threshold after which a <u>seizure</u> is considered <u>status epilepticus</u> differs according to the type of <u>seizure</u>:

* <u>Tonic-clonic seizures</u>: ≥ 5 minutes

* <u>Focal seizures with impaired consciousness</u>: ≥ 10 minutes

* <u>Absence seizures</u>: 10–15 minutes





### Etiology [[72]](/library/Ntc-dV0)




* Withdrawal from <u>antiepileptic drugs</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalance (e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>)

* Metabolic disturbances (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>uremia</u>, <u>porphyria</u>)

* Structural <u>brain lesions</u> and/or injury (e.g., tumors, trauma, <u>stroke</u>)

* <u>Anoxic</u> <u>brain injury</u>

* <u>Alcohol withdrawal</u>

* <u>Recreational drug</u> use

* Drug toxicity (e.g., from <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>, <u>isoniazid</u>)

* <u>CNS</u> infections (e.g., cerebral <u>malaria</u>, <u>neurocysticercosis</u>, viral <u>encephalitis</u>, <u>prion diseases</u>)

* Late-stage <u>neurodegenerative diseases</u> (e.g., <u>Alzheimer disease</u>)





### Classification [[71]](/library/YpXnL_)




* With prominent motor features 

* <u>Convulsive</u> (<u>tonic-clonic</u>)

* <u>Myoclonic</u> (with or without <u>coma</u>)

* Focal motor

* <u>Tonic</u>

* Hyperkinetic

* Without prominent motor features: nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) 

* With <u>coma</u>

* Without <u>coma</u>

* Absence

* Focal (e.g., <u>aphasia</u>, impaired consciousness, ongoing autonomic or sensory symptoms)





### Management




* See “<u>Management of acute seizures and status epilepticus</u>.”

* Maintain a high level of suspicion for NCSE: Consider continuous <u>EEG</u> and urgent <u>neurology</u> consult.  [[37]](/library/yicd8X0)





> [!WARNING]
> Consider NCSE in patients with persistently <u>altered mental status</u> following a <u>seizure</u> or with otherwise unexplained <u>altered mental status</u>, bizarre behavior, <u>autonomic dysfunction</u>, or sensory symptoms.




### Prognosis




* Mortality is bimodal, with the highest risk in <u>neonates</u> (25–39%) and patients > 80 years of age (> 50%). [[73]](/library/OtcIdV0)[[74]](/library/ltcvdV0)

* Overall <u>infant</u> and child mortality: 3.6% [[75]](/library/cpXao_)

* Overall adult mortality: 15.9% [[75]](/library/cpXao_)

---

## Epilepsy in pregnancy

> [!TIP]
> <u>Folic acid supplementation</u> is recommended in all individuals capable of <u>pregnancy</u>. [[81]](/library/46Y3OJ)




Information on other <u>seizure</u> disorders that can occur in <u>pregnancy</u> (e.g., <u>eclampsia</u>, <u>acute symptomatic seizure</u>) is detailed separately.




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[82]](/library/OGXIzz)[[83]](/library/5qci_W0)[[84]](/library/4G13zR0)




* Approximately 1.5 million female individuals of reproductive age in the US have <u>epilepsy</u>.

* Approximately 24,000 female individuals with <u>epilepsy</u> become pregnant per year.

* In the majority of cases, <u>pregnancy</u> does not affect <u>seizure</u> frequency.





### Etiology




Factors associated with an increased risk of <u>epileptic seizures</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> include:




* Reduced plasma concentration of <u>AEDs</u> due to physiologic changes in <u>pregnancy</u> (e.g., <u>steroid</u>-<u>hormone</u> induced hepatic enzyme induction, increased <u>renal clearance</u>)

* Psychosocial <u>stress</u>

* <u>Sleep deprivation</u>

* Hormonal changes (e.g., increased <u>estrogen</u>:<u>progesterone</u> <u>ratio</u>)





### Management [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[82]](/library/OGXIzz)[[84]](/library/4G13zR0)[[85]](/library/xqcE0d0)




#### General principles




* For all female individuals with <u>epilepsy</u> who are currently pregnant or expecting to be pregnant:

* Initiate <u>folic acid supplementation</u>. DOSAGE  [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[81]](/library/46Y3OJ)[[82]](/library/OGXIzz)[[86]](/library/xq1E0R0)[[87]](/library/s71tMR0)

* Counsel patients on the <u>teratogenic</u> potential of <u>AEDs</u> and the associated risks of adverse <u>pregnancy</u> outcomes. [[76]](/library/hL1cxh0)

* Consult <u>neurology</u> and <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> for obstetrical and drug management recommendations.

* If possible, obtain <u>AED</u> drug levels prior to <u>pregnancy</u> to determine a baseline level for continued monitoring. [[82]](/library/OGXIzz)

* Strict management of therapeutic <u>AED</u> levels during <u>pregnancy</u> is the gold <u>standard of care</u> for pregnant individuals with <u>epilepsy</u>. [[77]](/library/7714MR0)

* <u>Vitamin K</u> supplementation to prevent <u>vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn</u> (<u>VKDB</u>) [[85]](/library/xqcE0d0)[[86]](/library/xq1E0R0)

* All <u>neonates</u> should receive the standard dose of parenteral <u>vitamin K</u> supplementation at <u>birth</u>. [[86]](/library/xq1E0R0)[[88]](/library/sA1tOj0)

* There is insufficient evidence to support the use of prenatal <u>vitamin K</u> supplementation to prevent <u>VKDB</u> in <u>neonates</u> of patients on <u>enzyme-inducing AEDs</u>.

* <u>Epilepsy</u> alone is not an indication for <u>cesarean delivery</u>. [[77]](/library/7714MR0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Intrapartum</u> exposure to <u>teratogenic</u> <u>AEDs</u> is associated with a 2–3 fold increase in the likelihood of <u>major congenital malformations</u>. [[76]](/library/hL1cxh0)




#### <u>AED</u> management [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[82]](/library/OGXIzz)[[84]](/library/4G13zR0)[[85]](/library/xqcE0d0)[[87]](/library/s71tMR0)




Adjust <u>AED</u> regimen as needed in consultation with a <u>neurologist</u> to maximize <u>seizure</u> control and minimize <u>teratogenic</u> risk.  [[84]](/library/4G13zR0)[[87]](/library/s71tMR0)[[89]](/library/Bq1z0R0)




* Reduce <u>AED</u>-associated risk of <u>major congenital malformations</u> (MCMs).

* <u>AEDs</u> with low <u>teratogenic</u> risk: <u>lamotrigine</u> and <u>levetiracetam</u>

* <u>AEDs</u> with high <u>teratogenic</u> risk: <u>valproate</u> (highest risk), <u>phenobarbital</u>, <u>topiramate</u>, and <u>phenytoin</u>

* Monotherapy is associated with a lower risk of MCMs compared to polytherapy.  [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[90]](/library/H71KMR0)





##### In patients planning <u>pregnancy</u>




* Adjust <u>AED</u> therapy as needed early enough to: [[82]](/library/OGXIzz)

* Measure <u>AED</u> levels before <u>conception</u> (if possible) and determine the lowest effective dose

* Evaluate the <u>efficacy</u> of any new therapies

* Consult the treating <u>neurologist</u> before discontinuing <u>AEDs</u>.  [[91]](/library/RL1lxh0)





##### During <u>pregnancy</u>




* Measure <u>AED</u> levels regularly (e.g., monthly), especially for <u>AEDs</u> with increased clearance during <u>pregnancy</u>. [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[82]](/library/OGXIzz)

* Adjust target levels as needed, in consultation with <u>neurology</u>.





##### During the <u>postpartum period</u>




* Encourage <u>breastfeeding</u>; counsel patients regarding the following: [[82]](/library/OGXIzz)

* Overall, the <u>benefits of breastfeeding</u> outweigh the risks.  [[84]](/library/4G13zR0)[[86]](/library/xq1E0R0)

* Monitor <u>infants</u> for adverse effects of <u>AEDs</u> (e.g., sedation, poor sucking, <u>rash</u>).  [[90]](/library/H71KMR0)

* Adjust <u>AED</u> dosage in consultation with <u>neurology</u>; specialists may taper dosage to prepregnancy levels within 2–3 weeks after delivery.  [[90]](/library/H71KMR0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Valproate</u> is the <u>AED</u> associated with the highest risk of <u>major congenital malformations</u> and should be avoided, if possible, in patients with <u>epilepsy</u> who may become pregnant. [[57]](/library/ky1m2j0)[[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[82]](/library/OGXIzz)[[87]](/library/s71tMR0)




### Complications [[77]](/library/7714MR0)[[87]](/library/s71tMR0)




* Fetal complications

* Increased risk of <u>low birth weight</u> and small size for <u>gestational age</u> due to maternal <u>seizures</u>

* <u>Teratogenic</u> effects of <u>AEDs</u> (e.g., congenital <u>malformations</u>, abnormal neurocognitive development)

* Maternal complications: increased risk of the following

* <u>Preterm delivery</u>

* Need for <u>cesarean section</u>

* <u>Preeclampsia</u>

* Severe <u>postpartum hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Death</u> during delivery
